Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

Türkiye ve 14 ülkenin dışişleri bakanları, İngiltere ve Avustralya hükümetlerinin işgal altındaki Filistin topraklarında yürütülen yasa dışı İsrail yerleşim faaliyetlerine karşı, yerleşim inşasında rol alan şirketleri hedef alan tedbirler de dahil olmak üzere, yaptırım uygulama kararlarını memnuniyetle karşıladı.
Türkiye, Birleşik Arap Emirlikleri (BAE), Cezayir, Endonezya, Filistin, Katar, Kuveyt, Libya, Maldivler, Mısır, Nijer, Pakistan, Somali, Suudi Arabistan ve Ürdün dışişleri bakanları, İngiltere ve Avustralya'nın İsrail'in işgal altındaki Filistin topraklarındaki yerleşim faaliyetleri nedeniyle yaptırım uygulama kararına ilişkin açıklama yayımladı.
Açıklamada, İngiltere ve Avustralya'nın işgal altındaki Filistin topraklarında yasa dışı İsrail yerleşimlerinin inşasında faaliyet gösteren şirketler de dahil olmak üzere, yerleşim faaliyetleri nedeniyle yaptırım uygulama kararlarının memnuniyetle karşılandığı belirtildi.
İngiltere'nin Gazze'ye insani yardım ulaştırılmasını engelleyen bir kuruluşa yönelik yaptırım uygulama kararının da memnuniyetle karşılandığı aktarılan açıklamada, şunlar kaydedildi:
"Bu çerçevede bakanlar, E1 yerleşim planı dahil olmak üzere yerleşim faaliyetlerinden sorumlu kuruluş ve şahıslar ile yerleşimlerin genişletilmesini ve ilhak politikalarını destekleyen, kolaylaştıran veya hayata geçiren kuruluş ve şahıslara yönelik uygun uluslararası tedbirlerin alınması ve yaptırımlar uygulanması suretiyle hesap verebilirliğin sağlanmasına yönelik tüm çabaları desteklerini ifade etmektedir."
İsrail'in işgal altındaki Filistin topraklarında sürdürdüğü yerleşim politikalarının, özellikle E1 yerleşim planının ve işgal altındaki Doğu Kudüs'ün doğusunda yürütülen bağlantılı yerleşim faaliyetlerinin en güçlü şekilde kınandığı vurgulanan açıklamada, İngiltere ve Avustralya'nın söz konusu kararlarının uluslararası toplumun diğer üyelerini de benzer adımlar atmaya teşvik etmesi temennisinde bulunuldu.
Açıklamada, bu tedbirlerin, Birleşmiş Milletler Güvenlik Konseyinin (BMGK) 2334 (2016) sayılı kararı dahil uluslararası hukuk ve ilgili Birleşmiş Milletler kararları ile tüm devletlerin, İsrail'in hukuka aykırı işgali sonucunda ortaya çıkan durumu hukuki olarak tanımama ve işgalin yarattığı durumun sürdürülmesine yönelik yardım veya destek sağlamama yükümlülüklerini içeren Uluslararası Adalet Divanının 19 Temmuz 2024 tarihli İstişari Görüşü'yle uyumlu olduğu değerlendirmesinde bulunuldu.
İsrail'e yerleşim faaliyetleriyle bağlantılı olarak aldığı tüm tedbirleri ve işgal altındaki Filistin topraklarının coğrafi ve demografik yapısını değiştirmeyi amaçlayan diğer tüm uygulamalarını geri alma çağrılarının yinelendiği açıklamada, İsrail'in Gazze'de tırmandırdığı askeri gerilim kınandı.
Açıklamada, ABD Başkanı Donald Trump'ın güvenlik ve istikrarın tesis edilmesi, insani durumun ele alınması, yeniden imar ve toparlanma çalışmalarının kolaylaştırılması ve kalıcı barışın temellerinin atılması amacıyla Gazze'deki Çatışmayı Sona Erdirmeye Yönelik Kapsamlı Planı'nın eksiksiz ve derhal uygulanması çağrısında bulunuldu.
Gazze'nin işgal altındaki Filistin topraklarının ayrılmaz bir parçası olduğuna işaret edilen açıklamada, adil, kalıcı ve kapsamlı bir barışın tesis edilmesinin yegane uygulanabilir yolunun uluslararası hukuk ve ilgili Birleşmiş Milletler kararları uyarınca, 4 Haziran 1967 sınırları temelinde, başkenti Doğu Kudüs olan, bağımsız, egemen, coğrafi bütünlüğe sahip ve sürdürülebilir bir Filistin Devleti'nin kurulmasıyla gerçekleşecek iki devletli çözümün uygulanmasından geçtiğinin altı çizildi.

Watch: Fiona's care team hopes that a vibration plate will encourage a knit cap to make its way out of the hippo.
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.
"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said on Thursday afternoon.
Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017, swallowed the hat about 10 days ago and required emergency care.
The vet staff "tried everything they could to help her" but "it was ultimately too much to overcome", the zoo said.
Fiona initially seemed fine after swallowing the hat more than a week ago
"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".
The zoo also tried a different approach to attempt to get the hat to pass by encouraging Fiona to stand on a vibration plate platform borrowed from a local horse farm.
"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said.
Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Her death is also very premature, with hippos normally living up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo.
As well as being famous online, Fiona's story inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said Fiona "was a symbol of perseverance and joy" in the city.
"She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world," he wrote on X. "Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."

Zoo staff tried a colonoscopy, vibration plate and other procedures to aid the hippo in passing the hat to no avail
Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote in a post on social media .
With surgery too risky for full-grown hippos such as Fiona, who weighed in the region of 2,500lb (1,113kg), veterinarians tried an alternative method of getting the hat to pass through her system.
The hat fell near Fiona when a visitor to the Cincinnati zoo tossed it in the air, after which it bounced off a ceiling fan and fell into the enclosure, according to the Associated Press . Fiona ate the hat and was initially asymptomatic.
Days later, however, she began to lose appetite and staff at the zoo were forced to feed Fiona more in the hope that she would eventually get the hat through her digestive system.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the zoo statement said.
The zoo announced on Wednesday that the animal care team was using a vibration plate from a horse farm to help move things along, according to the Associated Press .
Fiona was sedated a second time on Tuesday for evaluation. After an ultrasound, veterinarians could see her intestines still trying to push the hat through. They also used a 9ft scope colonoscopy to view her intestines.
“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo had said on social media . Fiona remained out of her enclosure while she was receiving treatment.
Footage from the procedure released by the zoo on Wednesday shows her snorting and moving around her enclosure, which vets said was a sign of progress. Her hydration levels were being monitored.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked, and they were happy to see her respond. Thank you for your continued love and concern for Fiona and her dedicated care team,” the zoo said .
This wasn’t the first time Fiona’s health had been at risk. She became a global sensation after her premature birth in 2017, when she couldn’t stand on her own.
Hopes for Fiona’s recovery had garnered support from across the country including, apparently, from Timothy, another hippo at the San Antonio zoo. Timothy had sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
Zoo staff published a message on social media reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
Fiona was born six weeks premature at just 29lb (13.2kgs), falling below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time. Because she was initially too weak to nurse, Cincinnati Zoo staff hand-milked her mother while documenting Fiona’s recovery through photos and videos that captivated the internet.
Her survival then offered a much-needed positive chapter for the zoo following months of intense public backlash over the fatal shooting of Harambe , the silverback gorilla killed after a child breached his enclosure.
Wildlife facilities have long warned of the dangers posed by foreign objects dropped or blown into animal habitats. Past incidents have demonstrated the fatal risks involved, including a rare antelope that choked to death on a plastic cap of a snack pouch at a Tennessee zoo two years ago, and a polar bear at a German zoo that died in 2014 after swallowing a visitor’s dropped jacket.

US President Donald Trump has “sharply questioned” European countries over their continued financial support for Ukraine during the country’s conflict with Russia.
The president unexpectedly phoned into a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday, according to the Politico publication, which heard from four European officials who were briefed on the discussion.

One of the officials said Trump bemoaned the fact that a lot of people are dying in the conflict, and a lot of money is being “wasted” on the nearly five-year-long war. That official also confirmed that the US leader believes Putin will cooperate with peace negotiations with Ukraine.

German chancellor warns peace talks without Europe’s involvement are doomed to fail, urging unity with Ukraine.
European leaders of the so-called “Coalition of the Willing” gathered in the German capital for talks intended to signal a united front in support of Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting happened hours after an unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, China, between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.
Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the Shenzhen meeting a “photo op”, warning that any deal made without Europe at the table would fail.
Merz said that “if it comes to peace negotiations, then we will be involved”, adding that such talks “can only be successful with Ukraine and Europe”.
Merz said he hoped to work as a “team with Kyiv and Washington” when they hold talks with Russia on ending the Ukraine war, although no announcement of when that would be has been made.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe is “ready to enter negotiations”, insisting that “a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia must come first”.
“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position,” Burnham added.
European countries have been angered after the European Union was largely sidelined in the United States’ stop-start negotiations with Russia and Ukraine.
However, Donald Trump’s son-in-law and peace envoy Jared Kushner said, “Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side.”
Kushner said, “We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war.”
Russia is “comfortable”, Kushner added, with the idea of security guarantees for postwar Ukraine modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” he said, adding that Trump was “open” to the idea but that “obviously it has to be in America’s interest” and part of “a broader security package”.
It was not clear what form any guarantees would take, or whether Russia and Ukraine would accept them. Russia has not commented on Kushner’s claim.
Kushner said Trump called into the Berlin talks after his meeting with Putin, and that the last round of talks, in Abu Dhabi last week, produced no major breakthrough.
The British prime minister welcomed the US presence at talks in Berlin, saying it added momentum to end the war.
“This clearly has got to be a moment ⁠to move towards ⁠peace because of the US involvement that we’ve ⁠seen today and ⁠the progress clearly ⁠that is being made,” Burnham said.
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to ramp up efforts to end the war.
“Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
“Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said. NATO membership for Ukraine is among the issues holding back a peace deal for Ukraine.
In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, “We do not want Russia to drag all of this out into the winter. Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia.”
Speaking to reporters in Shenzhen, Putin vowed to retaliate for what he called serious damage to the Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland, in three Ukrainian aerial attacks this week.
“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin said.
He said the road section was “seriously damaged” but would be rebuilt, and that the bridge was a civilian asset that he had ordered closed to military hardware and ammunition.
Train traffic resumed on Thursday afternoon, RIA Novosti reported. Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said Russia would now have to move fuel and ammunition over land, “where our drones are waiting for the cargo”.
Putin said the Kremlin was not against European participation in peace talks and even proposed they be held in the Russian capital.
He said Moscow had proposed, through diplomatic channels, that European officials come to Moscow “to determine their position”, without setting a date.
Overnight, Russia’s Defence Ministry said it intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones. A Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Saratov region killed three people, local governor Roman Busargin said, and Ukraine said Russian anti-ship missiles and 98 drones hit 18 locations, killing two people and wounding at least 23.
Minor damage was reported at the Dutch and Austrian embassies in Kyiv.
The Netherlands summoned Russia’s ambassador in The Hague after the incident in which a projectile landed behind the building on Thursday afternoon. No one was hurt.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen told the broadcaster RTL the incident was “unacceptable”.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said Austria’s embassy in Kyiv was also hit, with no staff harmed, and Sweden said it would summon Russia’s ambassador over an explosion near its embassy, Reuters reported.
Russia’s embassy in the Netherlands had said earlier on Thursday that it was becoming “increasingly difficult to regard the Netherlands as a mere bystander” in the war. That followed a statement by the Dutch defence company Destinus that its missiles were the only foreign-made weapons used in Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch Bridge on Tuesday.

European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen , south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Several buildings were damaged in the latest Russian attack on Ukraine's capital Kyiv
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.
Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

Trump alleges defamation by three Times reporters and Penguin Random House in campaign against news outlets
A federal ⁠judge in Florida on Thursday said Donald Trump’s $15bn defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and book publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory ⁠for the US president in his ⁠legal campaign ​against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.
US district judge Steven Merryday in Tampa dismissed two claims in the suit while allowing core defamation claims to move forward.
The president’s claim against the publishers alleges defamation by three New York Times reporters – Susanne Craig, Russ Buettner and Peter Baker – in two articles published by the outlet and a 2024 book Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father’s Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success, which was co-authored by Craig and Buettner.
Trump claims the articles and book contain false statements that damaged his businesses and personal reputation. An earlier, 80-page version of the complaint was thrown out because it did not contain a concise summary and was filled with “vituperation and invective”, the court said.
An amended, 40-page complaint was filed in October last year that removed references to the 2024 presidential election. Mediation talks failed, along with a request by the defendants to move the action to federal court in New York.
The Times and Penguin have denied defaming Trump and said in a court filing that his case is legally flawed and aimed at scoring political points.
In dismissing two of Trump’s claims, Merryday, an appointee of George HW Bush, said the rest of his complaint plausibly alleged that statements accusing ​Trump of “planning and perpetrating complex crimes” were “based on incomplete, minimal information”.
In his claim, Trump cited 22 statements from a ⁠book by Baker and 12 from the articles ​by Craig and Buettner. They include assertions about Trump’s role in ​creating his hit reality ‌TV show The Apprentice, ​his inheritance from ​his father, his business ventures, and his upbringing in New York .
Representatives for the New York Times and Penguin Random House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesperson for the Times, has previously said “the lawsuit remains obviously meritless”. A spokesperson for Penguin Random House has also described the action as “meritless” and said it “stands by the book and its authors”.

Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.
Four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.
Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.
However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.
The Senegalese navy said it had rescued more than 1,400 people on Monday and Tuesday this week.
As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

The lawsuit cited a book about Trump by two NYT reporters and what it said were ‘false, malicious, defamatory’ articles.
A federal judge has said United States President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and book publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory for Trump in his legal campaign against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.
US District Judge Steven Merryday, an appointee of former President George HW Bush, handed down the ruling in federal court in Tampa, Florida, on Thursday.
Trump has filed several lawsuits against media companies since 2024, alleging they defamed him or fraudulently misled the public with false coverage. His critics have denounced the lawsuits as attacks on the free press.
The lawsuit against The New York Times and Penguin Random House cited a book about Trump by two New York Times reporters and what it characterised as “false, malicious, defamatory, and disparaging” articles that he says were aimed at sabotaging his chances in the 2024 presidential election, which he won.
The Times and Penguin have denied defaming Trump and said in a court filing that his case is legally flawed and aimed at scoring political points.
Representatives for The New York Times, Penguin Random House and Trump’s personal lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Merryday threw out two of Trump’s claims but said the rest of his complaint plausibly alleged that statements accusing Trump of “planning and perpetrating complex crimes” were “based on incomplete, minimal information”.
The lawsuit against The Times and Penguin concerned two articles and a book that cast doubts on his origin story as a savvy businessman who ascended in the real estate and entertainment industries.
Trump cited 22 statements from the book by Times journalist Peter Baker titled For Trump, a Lifetime of Scandals Heads Toward a Moment of Judgment, and 12 from the articles by Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner.
They include assertions about Trump’s role in creating his hit reality TV show The Apprentice, his inheritance from his father, his business ventures and upbringing in New York City.
The Times and Penguin said in a motion to dismiss that Trump’s lawsuit failed to explain how the statements were defamatory and included subjective opinions that cannot be proven true or false.
The latest victory comes days after another judge allowed Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC to move forward. That civil case alleges that the British broadcaster deceptively edited a documentary on the January 6, 2021, riots on Capitol Hill to damage Trump’s reputation.
Trump, since resuming office last year, has undertaken a wider pressure campaign against the media and coverage he disagrees with. He has an ongoing $10bn lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it had been dismissed. In September, he moved to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House and its press pool – a blanket ban a federal judge later blocked.
The US has fallen to a “ historic low ” in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) annual press freedom tracker, continuing a decade-long decline, the organisation said earlier this year in its annual report.
While the US, during the first year of Trump’s second term, remained in the “problematic” category, it dropped seven places from 57th in the world to 64th.
In a statement, Clayton Weimers, executive director of RSF’s North America office, said at the time that the US was experiencing a “press freedom crisis”.
“Trump and his administration have carried out a coordinated war on press freedom since the day he took office, and we will live with the consequences for years to come,” he said.

At least one person has died, and dozens more are missing after a boat carrying around 100 migrants capsized off the coast of Senegal while attempting to reach Spain, local officials have said.
The latest incident, which is thought to have happened in the early hours of Wednesday morning, comes amid a surge in departures towards the Canary Islands, with more than 11,000 people reaching the archipelago in the first half of November alone.
The boat, described by some sources as “rickety”, sank off the coast of Yenne, a town south of the Senegalese capital, Dakar.
“The accident happened around 3 a.m.," said Ousmane Sène, secretary general of the Yenne mayor's office.
Sène added that firefighters recovered one body while police arrested one survivor.
According to other survivors, there were around 100 people on board at the time it sank.
Sène confirmed that two other bodies were also recovered in nearby villages, but it’s not clear if they were people who drowned in this particular incident.
Recently, Senegalese coastal areas have become major departure points for migrants attempting the treacherous sea journey to Europe. Many of them are hoping to reach Spain’s Canary Islands, an archipelago off West Africa which lies more than 1,000 kilometres south of the European mainland.
According to Spanish government figures, more than 11,000 migrants reached the Canaries in the first half of November – that number was more than half the total for all of 2025.
This week’s sinking comes shortly after a disaster which saw at least 39 people die after a migrant boat sank near the town of Kébémer in northern Senegal.
Senegalese authorities are making efforts to crack down on people attempting the dangerous migration route and have made dozens of arrests.
On Wednesday, the country’s navy said it had “rescued” over 1,400 migrants at sea in just 48 hours.
Also on Wednesday, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye spoke out against the resurgence of migrant departures toward Europe and called for strengthened controls along Senegal's coasts, too.
“The acceleration and complexity of irregular migration demonstrate the urgency for the government to intensify... the diligent and efficient implementation of public policies concerning youth, education, vocational training, youth employment and entrepreneurship, as well as the economic empowerment of women,” said Faye.

Osian Morgan has previously appeared in Pobol y Cwm and Waterloo Road
Voicing Luke Skywalker in the Welsh-language version of Star Wars was a "dream job" according to actor Osian Morgan.
The Cardiff-born actor said he loved the film series as a child and playing one of the lead roles was "very exciting".
Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd - based on the original 1977 film Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope - was given its first showing at a red-carpet event in Cardiff on Thursday.
The dubbed Welsh version, featuring actors Matthew Rhys and Rhys Ifans, will be broadcast publicly for the first time by S4C on Christmas Day.
Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd (S4C, STAR WARS a Cymru Creadigol)
Almost half a century since A New Hope was first released, the sci-fi universe created by George Lucas remains one of the biggest film franchises of all time.
It has been translated into over 50 languages, with Welsh becoming its most recent.
"It feels very exciting, it's thrilling," said Morgan, who has previously starred in Welsh language soap opera Pobol y Cwm and in BBC drama Waterloo Road.
His family attended the first screening of Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd, and Morgan admitted his youngest brother had never seen any of the films before.
"Shout out to him because the first time he gets to see it in Welsh is great," he said.
The film's premiere in Cardiff included a rousing version of the theme tune
Mark Lewis Jones, who voices the dark lord Darth Vader, said on the red carpet it was "nice to record the voice but not have the make-up" and joked that "the Rhosllanerchrugog accent lends itself to the dark side".
Llyr Ifans, who plays C-3PO, said he hoped the film was successful and that more Welsh-language versions would follow.
"I'm quite confident it will go down well and there will be a lot of happy Welsh-speaking parents on Christmas Day."
Ifans said he been a fan of the Star Wars films since childhood, and getting invited to play the character was "surreal".
"When I first got the email through I thought 'wow, this is a bit weird doing Star Wars in Welsh' but playing C-3PO, one of the iconic parts, you can't say no, can you really?"
C-3PO is said to be fluent in six million forms of communication and Ifans said it was now one more.
Mark Lewis Jones, who voices Darth Vader, joked his accent 'lent itself to the dark side'
Prominent actors have lent their voices to the film's most famous characters, including Matthew Rhys (Han Solo), Rhys Ifans (Obi-Wan Kenobi) and Aimee-Ffion Edwards (Princess Leia).
Other voice actors in the Welsh version include Nia Roberts, Ioan Hefin, Richard Harrington, Owain Arthur, Rhodri Meilir, Richard Elfyn and Steffan Donnelly. The film is directed by Ellyn Stern.
The Welsh language version was announced at the National Eisteddfod in Pembrokeshire in August
The Welsh-language version was announced at the National Eisteddfod in Pembrokeshire in August, with Lucasfilm co-president Lynwen Brennan saying the franchise was keen to expand its horizons.
"As someone who was born and raised in Wales, seeing the audience reaction to iconic Star Wars moments retold in the Welsh language was a moment of great pride," she said.
S4C chief executive Geraint Evans added that working with "one of the most iconic and influential film franchises of all time is a tremendous honour".
"It is a unique opportunity to introduce the Welsh language to new audiences around the world, while showcasing Wales and its exceptional creative talent on a global stage," he said.

Actors Mark Lewis Jones and Osian Morgan, who voiced characters in dub of 1977 film, among guests on red carpet
It has been a memorable few days for Wales. At the weekend, the men’s rugby team secured a historic win against New Zealand – their first victory over the All Blacks in more than 70 years. Then on Thursday evening came another culturally significant moment when Cardiff rolled out the red carpet to celebrate the first Welsh-language dub of the Star Wars franchise.
Stars of stage and screen who voiced the words of Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, C-3PO et al in Welsh (Cymraeg) over the original 1977 Star Wars film took the plaudits at the Cineworld Cardiff screening.
Among those on the red carpet was Mark Lewis Jones, who has appeared in shows ranging from The Crown to Game of Thrones and had a role in the 2017 Star Wars film The Last Jedi. In this version of Star Wars, he is a Welsh Darth Vader.
He said he thought Welsh was a good language for Vader. “It has an ancient, poetic sense. It gives him that status, that authority,” said Jones, who hails from the Wrexham area in north-east Wales . “I give all my characters north-east Wales accents,” he said.
Also taking a bow was Osian Morgan – well known in Wales for his appearances in the Welsh-language soap opera Pobol y Cwm – who voices Luke Skywalker.
“There’s so much excitement about this project and the cast is unbelievable,” Morgan said. “I think in Wales we’re on an upward trajectory and this instils a lot of hope. The future is exciting for Wales, particularly in the creative arts. The talent is vast.”
Asked if he felt the pressure of being Luke Skywalker, he said he was thrilled rather than nervous. “He’s had such an important impact on my life,” he said. Morgan was also pleased that his 10-year-old brother’s first experience of Star Wars would be in the medium of Welsh. “The fact that Luke tonight in the Welsh language can have that impact on kids here is fantastic.”
Rhys Ifans, who has appeared in Harry Potter and Spider-Man films, had the tough job of standing in for Alec Guinness as the Jedi master Obi-Wan Kenobi. Sadly, he did not make it to Cardiff for the event.
His brother, Llŷr Ifans, the Welsh voice of the droid C-3PO, was present, however, which was apposite as C-3PO is “fluent in over 6 million forms of communication” – including, clearly, Welsh.
Ifans said: “When I first heard about it, I thought: wow, what are we doing – Star Wars in Welsh? The idea has settled. C-3PO is a genius who speaks over 6 million languages. Now he speaks 6 million and one. He speaks the best language in the world.”
Asked what accent he used for his C-3PO, Ifans said: “There are no accents in space. But it’s more about the character. He lives on his nerves and speaks staccato. I had to bring in those aspects.”
The Welsh-language version of the 1977 film (subsequently retitled Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope) has been produced by Lucasfilm and Disney in collaboration with the Welsh-language broadcaster S4C and the Welsh government via its Creative Wales agency.
Its Welsh title is Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd (New Hope). Those not lucky enough to be at the screening in Cardiff will be able to hear the immortal line “May the Force be with you” in Welsh (“A boed i’r Grym fod gyda chi”) when the version is broadcast on S4C platforms on Christmas Day.
Thursday’s screening wasn’t as glitzy as a London or Los Angeles premiere, but it had charm. Côr Bechgyn Glantaf, a schoolboys’ choir from Cardiff, performed as the crowds – including many children – arrived and made their way up the escalators of the multiplex to screens eight and nine. Band Pres Llareggub, which bills itself as a Bronx hip-hop-inspired, New Orleans-tinged brass band with attitude from north Wales, also provided a musical backdrop.
S4C’s chief executive, Geraint Evans, described the screening as a “hugely proud moment”. He said: “Most importantly, it will give Welsh-speaking children the thrill of hearing some of cinema’s most beloved characters speak their language for the very first time, showing that Welsh can tell any story.”
There are a few connections linking Wales and Star Wars, not least that a version of the Millennium Falcon was built in south-west Wales .
Mark Williams, who oversaw an exhibition about the Millennium Falcon, said he felt the Welsh-language version of the film was long overdue. “I’ve been saying for years it should be done, especially with the ties that Wales has with the franchise,” he said.
Also at the screening was the cabinet minister for enterprise, connectivity and energy in the Welsh government, Adam Price, who said it was an excellent opportunity for Welsh actors and production staff to work with a major Hollywood studio.
“Seeing one of the most iconic films of all time in Welsh is a great way to make the language more accessible and introduces it to new audiences beyond our shores,” he said.
The Welsh government is aiming to have a million people speaking Cymraeg by 2050. A spokesperson for the Welsh language commissioner’s office said one of its key aims was to increase the use of the language on a community level.
The spokesperson said: “In order to do this, the language must be seen and heard in all aspects of our daily lives. The use of Welsh in such a high-profile film as Star Wars has the potential to attract new audiences and raise awareness of the language.”

President Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP hide caption
SHENZHEN, China, and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday. Their meeting capped two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even though some of those powers had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.
"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," Xi said in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."
Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."
"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.
Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders laying out divergent agendas going in:
Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.
There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to smuggle in high-end Nvidia chips .
In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.
Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.
Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.
Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.
"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.
"We've known each other for a long time," Trump added after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."
Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."
Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.
The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.
For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.
Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.
Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.
Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.
Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.
Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.
The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.
Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches — both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.
From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.
In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.
Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.
Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.
The catch: His Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.
Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.
A joint declaration released after the talks on Thursday did state that the three leaders "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." It said their governments would "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons," but did not provide a time frame.
Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.
Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.
Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."
Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean Peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.
The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 19. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.
Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.
Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.
But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.
"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."
For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.
The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.
Judges of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) attend a public hearing ahead of the reading of the court's judgment in the genocide case brought by Gambia against Myanmar, in The Hague on Thursday. Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.
"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."
She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."
Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."
"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."
Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.
Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling over whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar, on Thursday. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.
She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel , on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.
"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.
The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.
In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.
Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.
The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.
But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.
In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online , "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.
Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."
The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.
However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.
The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.
Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.
Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.
Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.
"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.
She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.
Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu
The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road , Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza .
The operation lasted about 24 hours and on Thursday the military said it had been “completed”.
The IDF ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.
A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.
Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.
After the statement from the IDF that it had concluded the tank raid to dismantle a suspected Hamas tunnel, the defence ministry’s body in charge of civilian affairs in Palestinian territories, Cogat, said Palestinians would again be free to move in the targeted areas near al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps.
In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.
Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.
Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.
The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.
In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.
In June, an ⁠independent UN inquiry determined that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. A previous report by the commission in September 2025 found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza , and Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited those acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r:
Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.
That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.
Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.
"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.
Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families
Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.
At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

Suç temalı serinin yeni oyunu, bir önceki yapımın piyasaya sürülmesinden 13 yıl sonra geldi. 2013'te çıkan GTA V, satış rekorları kırarak tüm zamanların en çok gelir elde eden eğlence ürünlerinden biri haline gelmişti.
Seri, oyunculara suç dünyasında geçen bir hikâyenin parçası olma, araçları parçalama ve kurgusal ABD kentlerinde istedikleri kişilerle çatışmaya girme imkânı sunuyor. Oyunun dünyasında suçlular, seks işçileri ve toplumun kıyısında yaşayan karakterler önemli yer tutuyor.
GTA VI, yerel saatle gece yarısında ilk olarak Yeni Zelanda'da piyasaya çıktı. Oyun, her ülkede gece yarısına ulaşılmasıyla birlikte dünya genelinde erişime açıldı.
Yeni Zelandalı Luke Starik, oyunu deneyen ilk oyuncular arasındaydı ancak karakteri fazla uzun süre hayatta kalamadı. Starik, AFP'ye gülerek, "Şimdiden öldüm. İlk karakter uzun süre dayanamadı," dedi.
Tokyo'yu ziyaret eden Avustralyalı öğrenci Riley Fennel ise AFP'ye, "Bu hayatımdaki büyük olaylardan biri. GTA'yı çok uzun zamandır oynuyorum," diye konuştu.
İnceleme derleyicisi Metacritic, oyuna 100 üzerinden 99 puan verdi.
Almanca yayın yapan bir Reddit forumunda yazan 42 yaşındaki bir oyuncu, oyunu gece boyunca oynayabilmek için işten izin aldığını anlattı. Ancak saat 01.20'de baş ağrısı nedeniyle yatağa girmek zorunda kaldığını, buna rağmen oyundan çok etkilendiğini belirtti.
Oyuncu, "On üç yıl önce böyle bir oyunla sabah altıya kadar oynardım," diye yazdı.
Oyunun resmi Reddit forumunda da kullanıcılar, deniz motosikletini yeniden suya itebilmek gibi ayrıntılı etkileşim özelliklerini övdü. Bir kullanıcı, "Bu inanılmaz!" yorumunu yaptı.
Analiz şirketi Omdia, GTA VI'nın yıl sonuna kadar oyunun geliştiricisi Rockstar Games ve ana şirketi Take-Two Interactive'e 3,2 milyar dolar (2,9 milyar euro) gelir sağlayabileceğini tahmin ediyor.
PlayStation, oyunun çıkışının ardından durum sayfasında kısa süreli bağlantı sorunları bildirdi. Daha sonra hizmetlerin yeniden normale döndüğü açıklandı.
The Verge'de yayımlanan "GTA VI does something impossible - it lives up to the hype" başlıklı incelemede Andrew Webster, oyunun beklentileri karşıladığını belirterek, "Oyun o kadar iyi ki, etrafındaki büyük beklenti onunla ilgili en az ilginç şey," diye yazdı.
Sosyal medya kullanıcıları özellikle oyunun grafiklerine dikkat çekti.
Reddit kullanıcısı No_Strike9652, "Spoiler vermeden söyleyeyim, ışığın karakterlerden birinin arkasına tam olması gerektiği gibi vurduğu bir an var. Gerçek bir insana baktığıma yemin edebilirdim," yorumunu yaptı.
New York Üniversitesi Stern İşletme Okulu profesörü Joost van Dreunen, oyun piyasaya çıkmadan önce AFP'ye yaptığı değerlendirmede GTA VI'yı eğlence sektöründe benzeri az görülen bir yapım olarak nitelendirdi.
Omdia analisti James McWhirter ise oyunun etkisinin video oyunları sektörüyle sınırlı kalmayabileceğini söyledi.
McWhirter, "Oyunun erişim alanı o kadar geniş ki, akış platformları gibi diğer eğlence hizmetlerindeki kullanıcı etkileşimini de olumlu yönde etkileyebilir," değerlendirmesinde bulundu.
Çok sayıda hayran, Florida'dan esinlenerek tasarlanan kurgusal Leonida eyaletini keşfetmek için işten izin aldı.
Berlin'de yaşayan 27 yaşındaki Ukraynalı oyuncu Dmytro Shkambara, ilk oyun seansını uzun zamandır planladığını belirterek, "Dört gün izin alacağım," dedi.
İnsan kaynakları platformu Remote, 19 Kasım için dünya genelindeki izin taleplerinde yüzde 32 artış kaydedildiğini açıkladı.
Önceki oyunlardan daha büyük, daha gelişmiş ve daha gerçekçi bir deneyim sunacağı belirtilen GTA VI, Miami'den esinlenerek yaratılan suç dünyasının merkezindeki Vice City'de geçiyor. Oyunun hikâyesi, Bonnie ve Clyde'ı anımsatan bir suçlu çifti, Lucia ve Jason'ı konu alıyor.
Oyun, salı günü ABD'de düzenlenecek The Game Awards töreninde 8 dalda aday gösterildi. Yılın en iyi video oyunlarının ödüllendirileceği tören 10 Aralık'ta yapılacak.
Rockstar, oyunu geliştirmek için 8 yıldan fazla zaman harcadı.
Stüdyo, çalınan oynanış görüntülerinin çevrimiçi yayınlandığı 2022'deki bir hacklemeden sonra çıkışı iki kez erteledi ve geçen yaz yeni bir sızıntı dalgasıyla yeniden karşı karşıya kaldı.
Seri, uzun süredir şiddeti ve suçu yüceltmekle suçlanıyor. Aynı zamanda Amerikan toplumunun kusurlarını alaya almasıyla bilinen, sisteme başkaldırının bir pop kültür simgesi haline geldi.
Oyuncular, yayaların üzerinden geçebiliyor, uyuşturucu satabiliyor ve polise ateş edebiliyor.
King's College London'da dijital kültürler alanında ders veren Paolo Ruffino, "Bu seri, şiddeti ve farklı istismar ya da taciz biçimlerini, toplumsal cinsiyeti temsil etme biçimiyle her zaman aşırılığa kaçmasıyla ünlü," dedi.
Ruffino, "Tamamen yeni bir şey olmadığı sürece mutlaka büyük tartışmalar beklemiyorum," diye ekledi.
Rusya, Çin, Lübnan veya Katar'da şu an için resmi bir çıkış tarihi bulunmuyor.
